overview: Megasphaera is a genus of strictly anaerobic, Gram-negative cocci (family Veillonellaceae) that ferment lactate and sugars to short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate, valerate). In tuberculosis it has been reported as enriched in the sputum/airway microbiome of active-TB patients relative to contacts, where its SCFA output is hypothesized to skew local immunity toward anti-inflammatory, tolerogenic responses that may dampen anti-Mtb defense; it is also a normal commensal of the gut and oral cavity.
metallome: As an obligate anaerobe, Megasphaera relies heavily on iron-sulfur biochemistry: its energy metabolism is built around [4Fe-4S] ferredoxin and flavin-based electron-bifurcating systems, notably the butyryl-CoA dehydrogenase/electron-transferring flavoprotein (Bcd/EtfAB) complex that couples NADH oxidation to crotonyl-CoA reduction and ferredoxin reduction, so iron demand is substantial and is met preferentially from the more soluble ferrous (Fe2+) pool that predominates in anoxic niches. M. elsdenii also possesses an oxygen-sensitive [FeFe] (iron-only) hydrogenase, a non-heme enzyme shown to carry roughly 12 iron atoms and 12 acid-labile sulfides per molecule, which channels reduced ferredoxin to H2 production. A well-characterized feature of M. elsdenii is an FMN-containing flavodoxin that can serve as a one-electron carrier in place of ferredoxin; flavodoxin substitution for ferredoxin is a recognized iron-sparing strategy in iron-limited microbes, and M. elsdenii flavodoxin is a classic structural model, though iron-regulated induction of this swap is best documented in cyanobacteria and Bacillus rather than in Megasphaera specifically. In the TB airway, host nutritional immunity is relevant context: macrophages restrict iron, manganese, and zinc while also poisoning the phagosome with excess copper and zinc, the same metal-restriction/intoxication environment that drives Mtb's own IdeR (iron) and Zur (zinc) regulons, though genus-specific siderophore, metalloregulator, and metal-efflux systems for Megasphaera are not well characterized. Direct, Megasphaera-specific metal-transport and antioxidant (e.g., rubredoxin/rubrerythrin-type) data are limited, so the strongest claims here rest on its well-documented Fe-S, hydrogenase, and flavodoxin electron physiology.

overview: Mycobacterium is a genus of aerobic, acid-fast actinobacteria with a distinctive mycolic-acid-rich, lipid-dense cell envelope; it includes the obligate pathogen M. tuberculosis, the etiologic agent of tuberculosis. In the TB airway signature this genus is increased in sputum/lung samples, reflecting active pulmonary infection where the organism replicates within alveolar macrophages and granulomas rather than as a resident commensal.
metallome: Iron is central to mycobacterial physiology: M. tuberculosis scavenges Fe(III) from host iron sources (transferrin, lactoferrin, ferritin, and heme) using the salicylate-derived siderophores mycobactin (cell-associated) and carboxymycobactin (secreted/exochelin-like), with ferri-carboxymycobactin uptake via the IrtAB ABC transporter, whose IrtA FAD-binding domain reduces Fe(III) to Fe(II); siderophore biosynthesis and IrtAB are essential for intramacrophage survival and virulence. Iron-responsive gene expression is governed by the master regulator IdeR (a DtxR-family Fe-dependent repressor), which represses the mycobactin (mbt) biosynthesis and siderophore genes when iron is replete and de-represses them under the iron starvation imposed by host nutritional immunity. The host both withholds iron and manganese (e.g., NRAMP1/SLC11A1-mediated divalent-cation transport at the phagosome, calprotectin sequestration) and weaponizes metals by pumping toxic copper and zinc into the M. tuberculosis-containing phagosome. Mycobacteria defend against copper poisoning through the Cu-sensing regulator CsoR, which controls induction of the P-type ATPase CtpV and the outer-membrane channel protein MctB to extrude copper, both required for full virulence. Resistance to zinc poisoning requires the P1B-type ATPase CtpC together with the metallochaperone PacL1; ctpC is induced by zinc excess and a ctpC mutant accumulates zinc, is hypersusceptible to zinc, and is attenuated intracellularly (CtpC's in vitro substrate specificity is debated, but functionally it supports zinc efflux). The organism also relies on metalloenzyme antioxidant defense, notably a secreted iron-cofactored superoxide dismutase (SodA/FeSOD) and a peripherally localized Cu,Zn-SOD (SodC), to survive the macrophage oxidative burst.

overview: Prevotella is a genus of Gram-negative, obligately anaerobic Bacteroidetes that are dominant members of the oral and upper-respiratory microbiota and a normal constituent of the gut. In pulmonary tuberculosis it is repeatedly reported as enriched in sputum/airway communities and is regarded as part of a progression-associated dysbiotic signature, where its expansion accompanies increased airway inflammation (though Prevotella-driven inflammation is generally milder than that of frank pathogens). It is also a marker taxon in TB gut-microbiome shifts during anti-TB chemotherapy.
metallome: Like other host-associated Bacteroidetes (Bacteroides, Porphyromonas), Prevotella is strongly iron- and heme-dependent and lacks the genes to synthesize protoporphyrin IX de novo, so it must scavenge porphyrin/heme and inorganic iron from the host. Prevotella intermedia binds hemoglobin via an approximately 60 kDa outer-membrane protein (Kd ~1.5x10^-8 M, with strongest binding at acidic pH ~5) and uses a cysteine protease (interpain A) to oxidize and degrade hemoglobin and liberate heme as an iron source; cooperative heme capture in which the Porphyromonas gingivalis HmuY hemophore works together with P. intermedia interpain A has also been described. As Gram-negatives, members of this clade acquire heme/iron through TonB-dependent outer-membrane receptors and assimilate liberated ferrous iron through Feo-type (FeoAB) systems, with iron-uptake genes generally held under Fur-family (Fe2+-sensing) transcriptional repression. This heme/iron requirement places Prevotella against host nutritional immunity: hypoxic, hemorrhagic, iron- and heme-rich inflamed airway niches (as in cavitary TB) favor heme-scavenging anaerobes, whereas host sequestration of free iron and heme constrains them. Direct, species-specific data on zinc (Zur), manganese, and copper handling in Prevotella are limited, so those are inferred at the Bacteroidetes level rather than established for the genus.

overview: Alistipes is a genus of Gram-negative, bile-tolerant, strictly anaerobic rods in the family Rikenellaceae (phylum Bacteroidota), residing in the distal gut where it ferments amino acids and contributes to short-chain fatty acid (notably propionate/succinate) production. In the tuberculosis signature it is reported as increased: 16S gut microbiota studies find Alistipes (alongside Bacteroides and Blautia) enriched in latent TB infection (LTBI) in patients with poorly controlled diabetes, forming part of a six-taxon panel that discriminates LTBI from non-infected controls. Its enrichment correlates with altered systemic immunity (lower serum IL-17F and TNF-alpha), positioning it as a candidate gut biomarker rather than an airway colonizer.
metallome: As a member of the Bacteroidota, Alistipes is not expected to synthesize siderophores; the phylum is established as not producing siderophores, and the better-characterized gut Bacteroides instead rely on outer-membrane TonB-dependent transporters and a SusC/SusD-type apparatus to import iron, preferentially scavenging heme and host/dietary iron complexes rather than secreting high-affinity chelators. Bacteroidota commonly acquire iron via heme uptake (e.g., B. thetaiotaomicron prefers heme over soluble ferrous iron) and can pirate exogenous ferri-siderophores produced by neighboring microbes via the XusABC system characterized in B. thetaiotaomicron, an ecological strategy plausibly shared across bile-tolerant gut anaerobes including Alistipes. Intracellular iron homeostasis is generally tuned to repress uptake under iron-replete conditions, and both iron- and manganese-containing superoxide dismutases have been isolated from Bacteroidota (B. thetaiotaomicron), supporting survival of oxidative stress during transient oxygen exposure in the gut. Direct, species-level metallome data for Alistipes itself are sparse, so these requirements are extrapolated from established Bacteroidota/Rikenellaceae metal physiology. Because Alistipes acts in the gut compartment, its relevance to TB is via the gut-lung axis and competition for luminal iron/heme rather than direct participation in the macrophage phagosomal nutritional-immunity battle (Fe/Zn/Mn withholding and Cu/Zn intoxication) that shapes Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the airway.

overview: Campylobacter is a genus of microaerophilic, Gram-negative, spiral Epsilonproteobacteria best known as enteric pathogens (C. jejuni, C. coli) but also detected as oral/airway commensals (C. concisus, C. gracilis). In the tuberculosis signature it is reported as increased, clustering with Mycobacterium tuberculosis in sputum-microbiome meta-analyses and enriched in the diseased/co-infected airway, consistent with a broader dysbiotic shift toward facultative and microaerophilic taxa in the TB lung.
metallome: Campylobacter is heavily iron-dependent and its metal physiology is governed by the ferric uptake regulator Fur, which uses Fe(II) as corepressor to shut down iron-acquisition genes when iron is replete; a paralogous regulator, PerR, couples iron status to oxidative-stress defense. Although C. jejuni produces no siderophore of its own, it pirates exogenous chelates and host iron via multiple TonB-dependent outer-membrane receptors and ABC transporters: ferric-enterobactin (CfrA/CfrB with CeuBCDE), heme (ChuABCDZ), ferric-rhodotorulic acid (the periplasmic-binding protein P19/Cj1659 with Cj1658 and Cj1660-1663), and transferrin/lactoferrin-bound iron (CtuA with CfbpABC). Zinc is scavenged under host zinc restriction by the Zur-regulated, high-affinity ZnuABC importer, whose ZnuA orthologue is essential for growth in low-zinc environments and for chick colonization. Copper is detoxified by the Cu(I)-exporting P-type ATPase CopA (Cj1161) together with the periplasmic multicopper oxidase CueO (Cj1516), which oxidizes toxic Cu(I) to less-reactive Cu(II); both contribute to copper tolerance and host colonization. Reflecting its microaerophilic lifestyle, the genus relies on an iron-cofactored superoxide dismutase (SodB) rather than a Mn-SOD, so iron availability directly constrains its oxidative-stress resistance. These acquisition and efflux systems sit squarely against host nutritional immunity, in which calprotectin and lactoferrin sequester Fe/Zn/Mn while phagocytes weaponize Cu and Zn toxicity, making Fur/Zur-controlled metal homeostasis central to Campylobacter survival.
body site: Sputum/airway (also enteric/gut and oral as commensal niches)

overview: Eubacterium is a genus of obligately anaerobic, Gram-positive Clostridia (Firmicutes; Eubacteriaceae/Lachnospiraceae lineage) that are core commensals of the human colon and notable producers of butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) from dietary fiber fermentation. In the tuberculosis gut microbiome it is reported as increased in active TB relative to controls, alongside other SCFA-producing genera (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia), with this butyrate enrichment proposed to be immunologically counterproductive (butyrate dampens IFN-gamma/IL-17A and Th17 responses against M. tuberculosis). Its direction is context-dependent: enriched at the dysbiotic active-disease state but typically depleted by anti-TB antibiotic therapy, linking it to the gut-lung axis.
metallome: As a strict anaerobe, Eubacterium runs a fermentative, ferredoxin- and flavodoxin-based metabolism that depends heavily on iron-sulfur ([Fe-S]) cluster enzymes, making iron its dominant metal requirement. In the reducing, low-oxygen colonic lumen iron is present chiefly as soluble ferrous Fe(II), which Eubacterium and related gut Firmicutes acquire mainly through the Feo system (FeoAB; FeoB is the GTPase-driven ferrous permease) rather than the high-affinity siderophore systems typical of Proteobacteria; Eubacterium genomes are documented to carry feoA/feoB. Intracellular iron homeostasis is governed by a Fur-family ferric uptake regulator that, as Fe(II)-Fur, represses iron-uptake genes (including feoAB) when iron is replete. Like other anaerobic Firmicutes it generally lacks heme/cytochrome respiration and relies on manganese- or iron-cofactored superoxide dismutase for oxidative-stress defense. Genus-specific transporter and regulator data for Eubacterium are limited, so several assignments are extrapolated from well-characterized gut Clostridia such as Clostridioides difficile, where Fur-dependent FeoAB drives the principal ferrous-iron uptake and FeoB1 is required for full toxin production and pathogenesis (note: not all gut Clostridia encode Zur or MntR, so zinc/manganese sensing varies by taxon). At the host level the genus sits within the gut-lung-axis nutritional-immunity context of TB, where systemic iron sequestration (hepcidin-driven hypoferremia) and luminal metal availability shape which anaerobes thrive; Eubacterium's butyrate output is an immunometabolic rather than a metal-handling contribution to TB immunity.

overview: Kingella is a genus of fastidious, capnophilic Gram-negative coccobacilli in the family Neisseriaceae (class Betaproteobacteria), normally residing as commensals of the human oropharynx and upper respiratory tract; K. kingae is the best-studied species. In the tuberculosis airway it appears as a member of the disrupted oral/airway flora and has been reported as enriched in TB sputum (including higher abundance in multidrug-resistant TB) and in the broader expansion of oral-origin Proteobacteria in the dysbiotic, inflamed TB lung. It is not an etiologic agent of TB but a marker of the altered respiratory microbiome.
metallome: Genus-specific metallome data for Kingella are sparse, so its metal physiology is best inferred from the well-characterized Neisseriaceae family, where iron and zinc acquisition is dominated by TonB-dependent outer-membrane transporters rather than secreted siderophores (pathogenic Neisseria produce no known siderophores). In pathogenic Neisseriaceae these systems include transferrin-binding proteins (TbpA/TbpB) and lactoferrin-binding proteins (LbpA/LbpB) that pirate ferric iron directly from host glycoproteins, plus heme/hemoglobin uptake receptors, with expression repressed by the ferric-uptake regulator Fur under iron-replete conditions. The same lineage counters host nutritional immunity for zinc and manganese: zinc-piracy transporters TdfH and TdfJ extract Zn (and Mn, in the case of TdfH) directly from the neutrophil/NET protein calprotectin (S100A8/A9) and from S100A7, respectively, with expression controlled by the zinc-uptake regulator Zur. In the TB granuloma and phagosome the host imposes overlapping metal pressures—sequestering Fe/Zn/Mn via lactoferrin, transferrin and calprotectin, and depleting phagosomal divalent metals through NRAMP1/SLC11A1 efflux, while also weaponizing copper and zinc toxicity—so airway Neisseriaceae such as Kingella plausibly rely on these receptor-based metal-piracy and metal-homeostasis strategies, though direct experimental confirmation in Kingella itself is lacking.

overview: Streptococcus is a genus of facultatively anaerobic, catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci that are dominant commensals of the oral cavity and upper airway. In pulmonary tuberculosis it is consistently among the most abundant genera recovered from sputum (alongside Neisseria, Prevotella and Veillonella), but its direction is variable: relative abundance tends to be higher in less severe disease and falls relative to anaerobes such as Selenomonas and Fusobacterium in some patients with more advanced parenchymal disease. It is best regarded as an oral/airway taxon that is enriched yet inconsistent across TB cohorts rather than a driver of M. tuberculosis pathology.
metallome: Streptococci are notable for a manganese-centric metallome: because they are catalase-negative and lack a classical heme-based catalase defense, they rely heavily on imported Mn(II) (via the ABC importers PsaA/PsaABC in S. pneumoniae and MtsABC in group A streptococci) to populate Mn-dependent superoxide dismutase (SodA) and to buffer oxidative and peroxide stress, making Mn acquisition a key colonization/virulence determinant. Iron is obtained largely without a canonical siderophore program in most species; instead they use heme/iron ABC transporters, including heme-uptake systems (Shr/Shp surface proteins feeding the SiaABC/HtsABC transporter) and the dual Fe/Mn transporter MtsABC, with Fe/Mn-responsive uptake coordinated by the DtxR/MntR-family metalloregulator MtsR. Zinc homeostasis is governed by the Zn-sensing MarR-family repressor AdcR, which controls the high-affinity Zn importers AdcA/AdcAII and the polyhistidine-triad (Pht) proteins under Zn limitation, while the TetR-family activator SczA induces the CzcD efflux pump under Zn overload. These systems are direct targets of host nutritional immunity: neutrophil-derived calprotectin (S100A8/A9) chelates Mn(II) and Zn(II) to starve streptococci of both metals, and excess Zn can competitively displace Mn from the PsaA binding site, blocking Mn uptake and crippling Mn-SOD-mediated oxidative-stress resistance. Copper is handled mainly as a toxicity threat via the cop operon: CopA, a Cu(I)-effluxing P-type ATPase, with the CopY repressor and the CupA copper chaperone mediating detoxification rather than nutritional acquisition.

overview: Prevotella melaninogenica is a Gram-negative, black-pigmented obligate anaerobe of the phylum Bacteroidota and a core member of the oral and upper-airway commensal microbiota. In 16S rRNA surveys of tuberculosis sputum it is among the taxa reported enriched in TB patients relative to controls, consistent with the broader oral-to-airway dysbiosis and microaspiration that accompany pulmonary TB. Because its abundance in the lower airway is variable across TB cohorts and phenotypes, it is best read as a marker of an oral-flora/commensal airway shift rather than a direct TB pathogen.
metallome: Like other host-associated Bacteroidota (Prevotella, Porphyromonas, Bacteroides), P. melaninogenica is heme-auxotrophic: it lacks the enzymes for de novo protoporphyrin IX (PpIX)/heme biosynthesis and the classical siderophore pathways, so its iron acquisition centers on scavenging hemin/heme from host hemoproteins rather than on secreted siderophores. This dependence is why it requires hemin (with vitamin K) supplementation in vitro and accumulates a cell-surface iron(III)-PpIX (hematin-type) black pigment derived from host hemoglobin. Iron is liberated from heme by a dechelatase/demetallase activity, and in this bacterial family the released ferrous iron is taken up by the inner-membrane FeoAB ferrous-iron transporter (the route experimentally established for heme-derived iron assimilation in Bacteroides fragilis, alongside CobN-like BtuS proteins). This heme reliance places the organism against host nutritional immunity: hemoglobin/heme sequestration by haptoglobin and hemopexin, plus hepcidin-driven hypoferremia, restrict the heme-iron supply these anaerobes depend on. The accumulated ferri-heme surface pigment is itself protective, carrying intrinsic catalase-like activity that detoxifies hydrogen peroxide (relevant for an anaerobe under oxidative stress), though it also renders the cells susceptible to antimicrobial photodynamic inactivation. Species-level zinc, manganese, and copper handling in P. melaninogenica has not been experimentally defined; by family-level inference homeostasis would rely on conserved Zur-regulated zinc import and Mn/Fe transporters, but specific transporters have not been characterized. As a strict anaerobe it has limited need for the Mn-SOD/Cu-Zn-SOD oxidative-defense metalloenzyme repertoire emphasized in aerobic pathogens.

overview: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the obligate human pathogen and causative agent of tuberculosis. In this signature it is enriched in TB-patient sputum/airway — expected for the disease agent itself — where it replicates inside alveolar macrophages and granulomas rather than as a resident commensal.

The host both withholds iron and manganese (e.g., NRAMP1/SLC11A1-mediated divalent-cation transport at the phagosome, calprotectin sequestration) and weaponizes metals by pumping toxic copper and zinc into the M. tuberculosis-containing phagosome. Mycobacteria defend against copper poisoning through the Cu-sensing regulator CsoR, which controls induction of the P-type ATPase CtpV and the outer-membrane channel protein MctB to extrude copper, both required for full virulence. The organism also relies on metalloenzyme antioxidant defense, notably a secreted iron-cofactored superoxide dismutase (SodA/FeSOD) and a peripherally localized Cu,Zn-SOD (SodC), to survive the macrophage oxidative burst.

overview: Segatella oris (formerly Prevotella oris) is a Gram-negative, obligately anaerobic, saccharolytic member of the Bacteroidota/Prevotellaceae that normally resides in the human oral cavity (gingival sulci, periodontal pockets, dental biofilms). In tuberculosis it is one of the oral-origin anaerobes enriched in the diseased lower airway/sputum, reflecting the broader shift toward an anaerobic, oral-type community. It is regarded as a marker of the dysbiotic TB airway rather than a primary pathogen, and is not the causative agent of disease.
metallome: The dominant metallome feature is dependence on exogenous heme/iron: like other host-associated Bacteroidota (Bacteroides, Prevotella, Porphyromonas), Segatella/Prevotella spp. lack a complete de novo protoporphyrin IX (heme) biosynthesis pathway and require hemin (plus vitamin K/menadione) as growth factors, scavenging iron-protoporphyrin IX from the host. Prevotella oris produces a secreted thiol-activated hemolysin, providing a route to liberate hemoglobin-bound heme; related oral black-pigmented Prevotella (P. intermedia, P. nigrescens) accumulate a surface pigment of monomeric iron(III)-protoporphyrin IX (Fe(III)PPIX·OH, hematin). In the model Bacteroidota, iron released from heme is assimilated through the inner-membrane ferrous-iron transporter FeoAB together with the CobN-like proteins BtuS1/BtuS2 (demonstrated in Bacteroides fragilis). This heme/iron-foraging physiology sits within the host nutritional-immunity environment of the TB lung, where calprotectin and lactoferrin sequester Fe/Mn/Zn and the macrophage phagosome both withholds Fe/Mn (NRAMP1/SLC11A1) and deploys Cu and Zn toxicity against intracellular microbes. Species-specific data on zinc (Zur), manganese (Mn-SOD), and copper efflux for S. oris are lacking, so those details are inferred at the genus/family level rather than directly demonstrated.

overview: Arachnia propionica (reclassified as Propionibacterium propionicum and now Pseudopropionibacterium propionicum, Scholz and Kilian 2016) is a Gram-positive, aerotolerant anaerobic, filamentous/branching member of the family Propionibacteriaceae (phylum Actinomycetota) that is a normal commensal of the human oral cavity and upper respiratory tract. In tuberculosis it is reported as decreased/depleted in the sputum and airway microbiome, consistent with the broader loss of oral commensal Actinomycetota and anaerobes that accompanies TB-associated airway dysbiosis. Its decline is regarded as a marker of disrupted commensal community structure rather than a driver of disease.
metallome: Species-specific metal-handling data for P. propionicum are sparse, so its metallome is largely inferred from the well-characterized physiology of high-GC Gram-positive Actinomycetota (the lineage including Corynebacterium, Mycobacterium and the propionibacteria). In these organisms iron homeostasis is governed by a DtxR/IdeR-family metalloregulator that, when iron-replete, represses high-affinity iron-uptake systems (siderophore biosynthesis/transport and heme/Fe acquisition) to avert Fenton-chemistry toxicity, while derepressing them under iron limitation. Zinc acquisition and efflux are typically controlled by a Fur-family zinc uptake regulator (Zur), and manganese supports oxidative-stress defenses such as superoxide dismutase; notably, propionibacteria (e.g., Propionibacterium shermanii) make a cambialistic SOD that can use either Fe or Mn as cofactor, providing genus-level evidence of flexible Fe/Mn handling. Crosstalk between the Zur and DtxR/IdeR axes links zinc and iron status in this clade. As a mucosal commensal it must contend with host nutritional immunity, in which calprotectin and lactoferrin sequester Fe, Zn and Mn at airway surfaces; loss of such commensals in TB may reflect the metal-restricted, inflamed niche favoring M. tuberculosis, which itself deploys IdeR-controlled siderophores (mycobactin) and copper/zinc-handling systems to survive phagosomal Cu/Zn intoxication and Fe/Mn withholding. Direct evidence for siderophore production or specific metal transporters in P. propionicum itself has not been established.

overview: Cardiobacterium hominis is a fastidious, capnophilic, pleomorphic Gram-negative bacillus of the family Cardiobacteriaceae and the "C" of the HACEK group. It is a normal commensal of the human oral cavity, nose, and upper respiratory tract and is best known clinically as a rare cause of subacute infective endocarditis. In the tuberculosis signature it is reported as decreased, consistent with the broader depletion of oral/upper-airway commensals seen in TB-associated dysbiosis.
metallome: The most firmly established metal-related trait of C. hominis is its dependence on heme iron: on primary isolation it characteristically shows an apparent hemin (X factor) requirement, which—together with elevated CO2—enhances initial growth, although this requirement is typically lost on subculture (and can lead to misidentification as Haemophilus). This heme/porphyrin dependence indicates that, like other fastidious HACEK Gram-negatives, the organism relies on host-derived heme as an iron and porphyrin source rather than on robust de novo synthesis. Iron/heme import in such Gram-negatives canonically proceeds through TonB-ExbB-ExbD-energized outer-membrane receptors, but dedicated heme/iron transport, siderophore, and metal-homeostasis systems have not been annotated or characterized in C. hominis specifically (its draft genome describes no such systems), so any such pathway is inferred at the family level only. Notably, C. hominis is catalase-negative (and oxidase-positive), so it lacks the classic heme-dependent catalase used by many pathogens to detoxify peroxide, leaving it more reliant on other oxidative-stress defenses. Taxon-specific data on zinc (Zur), manganese, and copper homeostasis and the corresponding host nutritional-immunity interplay are likewise uncharacterized. Because this is a depleted oral commensal rather than the TB pathogen, its metallome is most relevant as a marker of niche disruption accompanying M. tuberculosis-driven dysbiosis, not as a direct effector of nutritional immunity.
body site: Oral / upper respiratory (oropharynx, nose); detected in sputum/airway sampling

overview: Solobacterium moorei is a Gram-positive, obligately anaerobic bacillus of the family Erysipelotrichaceae (phylum Firmicutes/Bacillota) and a commensal of the human oral cavity and gut; it is also an occasional opportunistic pathogen in bloodstream and wound infections. In the oral niche it ferments amino acids and is a recognized contributor to halitosis and periodontal disease, generating volatile sulfur compounds including H2S. In TB airway/sputum microbiome studies its direction is not firmly established: a published meta-analysis reported that Solobacterium clustered with (co-occurred with) Mycobacterium tuberculosis rather than being depleted, so any directional claim should be treated as uncertain.
metallome: No species-specific siderophore, heme-uptake, or dedicated iron-regulatory (e.g., IdeR/Fur-type) system has been experimentally characterized for S. moorei, so its metallome can only be inferred from its lineage as an obligately anaerobic, fermentative Firmicute. In the reducing, low-oxygen niches these organisms occupy, iron is available chiefly as soluble ferrous Fe(II), and anaerobic Firmicutes typically rely on FeoB-type ferrous-iron transporters rather than ferric-siderophore machinery, with Feo and other Fe(II)/heme uptake genes induced under anaerobic iron limitation. Manganese is generally acquired through NRAMP/MntH-family proton-coupled divalent-metal transporters (which can also move Fe(II)), and a Mn-leaning oxidative-stress posture is common in fermentative anaerobes that lack robust catalase/heme-based detoxification. Zinc homeostasis in this group is usually governed by Zur-regulated high-affinity ZnuABC-type uptake balanced against CDF/efflux exporters, and copper tolerance by Cu-translocating P-type ATPase (CopA) efflux. At mucosal surfaces these organisms are subject to host nutritional immunity—calprotectin- (Mn/Zn/Fe) and lactoferrin-mediated (Fe) sequestration—but all of the above are genus/family-level inferences, not S. moorei-specific measurements.
body site: Oral (tongue dorsum/saliva); also airway/sputum as an oral-derived commensal, and gut
